name: Brussels
meta_description: TDSC investigative consulting in matters touching Brussels: EU affairs counterparties, procurement integrity, association due diligence and court support.
hero_lede: Investigative consulting for matters touching Brussels, scoped from Nashville: background research on public affairs firms, associations and intermediaries around the EU institutions, procurement and grant integrity questions, and factual support for counsel before the Brussels enterprise courts and in CEPANI or ICC arbitration.
intro: Brussels is Belgium's capital region and the principal seat of the European Union institutions. The Brussels-Capital Region, made up of 19 municipalities, had 1,255,834 residents on 1 January 2026, of whom 36.7 percent were not Belgian nationals. It generated EUR 103.3 billion of GDP in 2023, about 17 percent of Belgium's output from under 11 percent of its population, and services account for over 90 percent of value added. At the end of 2024 more than 53,000 people worked for European and other international institutions in the region, alongside 7,268 diplomatic staff and 122,725 active VAT-registered enterprises. Hundreds of thousands of workers commute in daily from Flanders and Wallonia.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Brussels because it is where regulation, public money and representation meet. Companies engage public affairs consultants, trade associations and intermediaries whose backgrounds, funding and conflicts matter. Bidders and contracting bodies face integrity questions in EU and Belgian procurement and grant programmes. European headquarters located in the city deal with internal misconduct and whistleblower reports involving staff of many nationalities. Investors and counterparties need background research on individuals moving between public institutions and private practice. Litigants before the Brussels courts or in arbitration seated in the city need well-sourced facts about counterparties operating across several countries.

matters.title: Public affairs and intermediary background
matters.text: Background research on lobbying consultants, advisers and intermediaries a client proposes to engage in Brussels, covering ownership, other clients where public, prior roles in public institutions, media and litigation history, so that conflicts of interest and reputational exposure are understood before contracts are signed.

matters.title: Procurement and grant integrity
matters.text: Fact-finding for bidders, contracting bodies and counsel where EU or Belgian procurement or grant procedures raise questions about collusion, undisclosed links between bidders, subcontractor capacity or the backgrounds of consortium partners, using corporate records, published award notices and open sources.

matters.title: Association and NGO due diligence
matters.text: Research into the governance, funding and leadership of trade associations, foundations and non-profit bodies registered in Brussels before a client joins, funds or partners with them, identifying who directs them, who pays for them and whose interests they represent.

matters.title: European headquarters internal investigations
matters.text: Support to counsel investigating suspected fraud, conflicts of interest or misconduct at Brussels-based European headquarters, focusing on background research into vendors, consultants and associated companies and on structuring work in line with Belgian rules on investigations and GDPR.

matters.title: Revolving door and appointment checks
matters.text: Background research on candidates for senior roles, board seats or advisory positions who have worked for EU institutions, permanent representations or Belgian public bodies, to identify conflicts, restrictions publicly disclosed after leaving office and reputational issues relevant to the appointment.

local_context.title: Brussels enterprise courts
local_context.text: Commercial disputes between enterprises in Brussels go to the enterprise court, which sits in separate French-speaking and Dutch-speaking courts. The Dutch-speaking court reported around 10,000 new cases a year in 2019 and has also had national jurisdiction over certain matters such as patents, European trademarks and designs, and class actions. Past staffing shortages caused significant delays, which led some parties to prefer arbitration for ordinary commercial disputes.

local_context.title: Higher courts in the capital
local_context.text: The Brussels Court of Appeal hears appeals from the Brussels courts, and the Court of Cassation, Belgium's highest ordinary court, also sits in Brussels. Courts of first instance, rather than the enterprise courts, deal with provisional measures supporting arbitration and with annulment and enforcement of awards. A 2017 government plan for an English-language Brussels International Business Court did not, as far as we can confirm, result in an operating court.

local_context.title: CEPANI and arbitration in Brussels
local_context.text: CEPANI, the Belgian arbitration and mediation centre, is based in Brussels and administers domestic and international cases under its own rules, and ICC arbitrations are also frequently seated in the city. Practitioners have presented arbitration as a practical alternative when the enterprise court backlog is heavy. Investigative support in arbitration is confined to factual research for counsel and the parties.

local_context.title: Regional institutions and languages
local_context.text: The Brussels-Capital Region has its own government and parliament with powers over matters such as economic policy, employment, housing and regional procurement, alongside federal and EU bodies in the same city. Public records, court documents and company filings may be in French or Dutch depending on the language the party or authority uses, so research must cover both languages. Name variants in each language should be searched.

local_context.title: EU institutions as a source landscape
local_context.text: With over 41,000 people working for European institutions in the region, Brussels produces a dense public record: published procurement notices, register entries, institutional decisions and declarations by office holders. These can corroborate or contradict claims made by consultants, bidders or candidates. Research relies on what is lawfully public and does not seek internal institutional information. Findings are reported with their sources.

tdsc_approach: For matters touching Brussels, TDSC first identifies whether the question sits at EU, federal or regional level, because that determines which public records, procurement notices and courts are relevant. Research is conducted from Nashville using Belgian company publications, EU and Belgian procurement data, published decisions, association and institutional registers, and French, Dutch and English-language sources. Where interviews or document retrieval are justified, TDSC coordinates with qualified local professionals and the client's Belgian counsel rather than acting directly, and takes account of Belgian rules on private investigations. Personal data is processed only as the purpose requires, with GDPR obligations agreed with the client at the outset.

faqs.q: Can you vet a lobbying consultant before we hire them in Brussels?
faqs.a: Yes. We research the consultant's company, ownership, publicly disclosed clients and registrations, prior public roles, media coverage and litigation, and look for links to parties whose interests may conflict with yours. The aim is to identify reputational and conflict risks before engagement. We do not obtain confidential information about the consultant's other clients or communications.

faqs.q: How do you approach suspected collusion in an EU or Belgian tender?
faqs.a: We support counsel or compliance teams by mapping the bidders' ownership, directors, addresses and shared personnel, and by reviewing published award notices and prior contracts for patterns. Findings are presented as sourced facts. Whether conduct breaches procurement or competition rules is a question for counsel and, where relevant, the competent authorities.

faqs.q: Which Brussels court would hear our commercial dispute?
faqs.a: Disputes between enterprises usually go to the Brussels enterprise court, in its French-speaking or Dutch-speaking form depending on language rules, with appeals to the Brussels Court of Appeal. Many international parties choose CEPANI or ICC arbitration seated in Brussels instead. Your Belgian counsel will advise on forum; we support them with factual research.

faqs.q: Why do Brussels records come in two languages?
faqs.a: The Brussels-Capital Region is officially bilingual. Companies, associations and courts operate in French or Dutch, and filings or judgments follow the language used. A counterparty's documents may be in one language and its litigation in the other. Our research covers both, together with English-language EU material, so nothing is missed because of language.

faqs.q: Does TDSC have an office in Brussels?
faqs.a: No. TDSC is based in Nashville and has no office or staff in Brussels or elsewhere in Belgium. Most work is desk-based research using public and commercial sources. Where local steps are needed, we coordinate with qualified local professionals and the client's Belgian counsel, acting lawfully and within the agreed scope.
